content: Has the autogenerated .eq_def lemma always been a thing? I had the impression that for every definition X we write, we should normally add a lemma X_def as API, and this is present in many files. If X.eq_def is already autogenerated, should we delete all instances of X_def across mathlib?

I think it's not always possible, simp/rw have special handling for these, and I've seen them fail sometimes with the error Failed to rewrite using equation theorems. But I'm not sure.

Regardless of the technical issues, definitional lemmas are very useful for when the definition changes. Then the proof can change from rfl to something else, without breaking anything. So we instead of deleting them, we should add a lot more! (issue #31745)
Though it's debatable whether _def is a good naming convention for these.
I couldn't find any .eq_def in the doc. I guess they are automatically hidden?

I believe docgen intentionally triggers their generation, to make them show up in the search.
Although Loogle doesn't, and I've wanted to solve this for a year now (#new members > Loogle missing equations, although I might be confusing eq_def with eq_1, not sure)

Snir Broshi said:

Though it's debatable whether _def is a good naming convention for these.

Yeah, then I'd imagine we should rename the lemma to something that's not _def! Whereas eq_def is always syntactic equality?

Coincidentally, I also wanted to ask a question about eq_def today: Should it be considered an internal detail? Currently it isn't:

import Lean
/-- info: false -/
#guard_msgs in
#eval Lean.Name.isInternalDetail ``Function.Injective.eq_def

The context is the Lean declaration diff on PRs, which currently includes eq_def lemmas, but perhaps shouldn't. Thoughts?

Snir Broshi said:

Wdym by syntactic equality here?

Sorry I guess I meant definitional equality

Oh I think I understand: you mean we should keep using eq_def, but when changing the definition we should rename the lemma?
If so, then the issue is that then what do you do with the new definitional lemma for the new definition? You can't/shouldn't take over eq_def. So we're back to avoiding _def when naming.

I think eq_def should very much depend on the definition (because that's what it says), so if the definition changes so will (and should) this autogenerated definition, and we should never have any lemmas called _def. If a definition A is definitionally or propositionally equal to definitions B and C, then I guess we would (and should) have A.eq_def, A_eq_B, and A_eq_C? I guess I'm not phrasing this well, but we shouldn't care if A is definitionally or propositionally equal to B or C, but the lemma names should always be eq_B and eq_C, so the implementation remains hidden.
Doesn't docs#continuous_def say something which is not unfold Continuous? It unravels the one-field structure. I find continuous_def very helpful for teaching demos

Ah, maybe one-field structures are an exception. I'm really new to .eq_def, and seems like Continuous (or other structures) don't have autogenerated .eq_defs? Maybe one-field structures should have autogenerated .eq_defs that just unravels that one field?
Then my point still stands? We don’t need continuous_def

We certainly need it for teaching. There has been in the past some tension between "this tactic is useful for teaching" and "this tactic is subsumed by this much stronger one (which destroys all the teaching questions by solving them all in one go)"
So what you’re saying is continuous_def is easier a name than Continuous.mk_iff, which is fair.

David Ang said:

So what you’re saying is continuous_def is easier a name than Continuous.mk_iff, which is fair.

The @[mk_iff] attribute would create a lemma named continuous_iff. That is, it would if docs#Continuous were a structure instead of a def docs#Continuous is a structure, TIL
